report.releaseDate: 16 Oct 2026 (DICJ Q3-26 game-type statistics; monthly Sept GGR released 1 Oct 2026)
report.currency: MOP (Macau pataca; tables in MOP billions unless stated) with ~USD alongside at USD/MOP 8.07
report.verdict: Macau's casino GGR fell 3.8% YoY to MOP 60.22bn (~$7.46bn) in Q3-26 — the first quarterly decline since the post-COVID reopening — as mass/premium-mass baccarat dropped 7.9% and the market absorbed the World Cup, softer Chinese high-end demand and tougher hold comps; VIP stabilised (+6.3% QoQ, flat YoY) and slots grew 18.8%. For an operator, Macau remains a closed, six-concession, land-based-only market taxed at an effective 40% of GGR until 31 Dec 2032: the only realistic entry is B2B (EGMs, systems, content), where the slot segment is the one structurally growing line.
summary: **First quarterly YoY decline of the recovery cycle.** DICJ data for Q3-26 (Jul–Sep) put GGR from games of fortune at MOP 60.22bn (~$7.46bn), down 3.8% YoY and 1.3% QoQ, against an implied Q3-25 base of MOP 62.6bn (~$7.76bn). IAG rounds the same release to MOP 60.4bn/−3.7%; the AGB/Focus GN/Yogonet figure of MOP 60.22bn is used here.

**Mass/premium-mass baccarat is the problem line.** Mass baccarat GGR fell 7.9% YoY and 4.4% QoQ to MOP 33.61bn (~$4.17bn); its share of GGR slipped to 55.8% from 58.3% a year earlier. The MOP 2.88bn (~$357m) absolute drop exceeded the total market decline, i.e. everything else net-grew.
**Total baccarat (the Gaming Intelligence hook) was MOP 50.52bn (~$6.26bn), −5.4% YoY**, the lowest in six quarters; baccarat remains ~84% of casino GGR, underlining Macau's product concentration.

**VIP has stabilised rather than recovered.** VIP baccarat GGR was MOP 16.91bn (~$2.10bn), +0.1% YoY and +6.3% QoQ after an 18.8% sequential fall in Q2-26; share rose to 28.1%. 9M-26 VIP GGR is MOP 52.38bn (~$6.49bn), +9.9% YoY. Caveat: DICJ's VIP definition is table-designation based and runs far above the concessionaires' own VIP disclosures.

**Slots are the only structurally growing product.** Slot GGR rose 18.8% YoY to MOP 4.09bn (~$0.51bn), 6.8% of GGR (5.5% a year ago); 9M-26 slot GGR is MOP 12.18bn (~$1.51bn), ~+19% (derived). Live multi-game (LMG) electronic tables fell 8.0% to MOP 1.14bn (~$0.14bn).

**Monthly cadence shows four consecutive YoY declines.** July MOP 20.26bn (~$2.51bn, −8.4%, World Cup final 19 Jul), August MOP 21.89bn (~$2.71bn, −1.2%), September MOP 18.06bn (~$2.24bn, −1.2%, lowest month of 2026, −17.5% MoM). 9M-26 GGR is MOP 187.1bn (~$23.2bn), +3.2% YoY but ~15% below 9M-19's MOP 220.3bn (~$27.3bn).

**Channel: 100% land-based.** Macau licenses no online casino or online betting; online penetration of the regulated market is 0%. Non-casino regulated wagering is limited to the Macau Slot sports lottery (football GGR MOP 152m/~$18.8m, +49% on the World Cup; basketball MOP 44m/~$5.5m, +4.8%) and the SLOT Chinese lottery; horse racing ceased in 2024.

**Licensing is closed until 2032.** Law 16/2001 as amended by Law 7/2022 caps the market at six concessions (SJM Resorts, Galaxy Casino, Venetian Macau/Sands China, Wynn Resorts (Macau), Melco Resorts (Macau), MGM Grand Paradise), each a 10-year contract from 1 Jan 2023 to 31 Dec 2032, extendable by up to three years only exceptionally. Market-wide caps: 6,000 tables and 12,000 machines.

**Tax base is GGR, effective rate 40%.** Special gaming tax 35% of GGR (art. 27) plus fixed contributions of 2% (public foundation) and 3% (urban development, tourism, social security) — Law 7/2022 removed the former 'up to' wording, lifting the levies from an actual 4% to a fixed 5%. The 5% can be waived on GGR from foreign (non-Greater-China) players under AR 54/2022. Gaming profits are exempt from complementary (profits) tax through 31 Dec 2027.

**Premiums and minimum-yield rules add a fixed-cost floor.** Each concessionaire pays a fixed premium of MOP 30m (~$3.7m) p.a. plus MOP 300,000 (~$37k) per VIP table, MOP 150,000 (~$18.6k) per mass table and MOP 1,000 (~$124) per machine (minimum charge equivalent to 500 tables/1,000 machines). A 'special premium' of 35% of any shortfall applies if annual GGR per table is below MOP 7m (~$0.87m) or per machine below MOP 300,000 (~$37k).

**Fiscal take is running ahead of GGR.** The Financial Services Bureau collected MOP 74.56bn (~$9.24bn) of gaming taxes in 9M-26, +5.9% YoY (tax lags GGR by one month), equal to 84.1% of the government's MOP 88.71bn (~$10.99bn) current revenue and 80.6% of the MOP 92.53bn (~$11.47bn) full-year budget (of which MOP 82.60bn/~$10.24bn is the 35% special tax; junket-commission tax budgeted at just MOP 150m/~$18.6m).

**Government forecast is a floor, not a target.** The 2026 budget assumes GGR of MOP 236bn (~$29.2bn); Chief Executive Sam Hou Fai said on 10 Oct that no downward revision is being considered. With 9M-26 at MOP 187.1bn, Q4 needs only MOP 48.9bn (~$6.06bn), or MOP 16.3bn (~$2.02bn)/month — a bar the market will clear even in a severe Q4.

**Sell-side is converging on ~+1% for FY26.** J.P. Morgan cut FY26 to MOP 249bn (~$30.9bn, +1% vs FY25's MOP 247.4bn/~$30.7bn, ~85% of 2019); Seaport models Q4 −5%; Bloomberg consensus growth has fallen to ~3% from 7% at the start of the year; one bank's October call is −6% to MOP 22.6bn (~$2.80bn).

**Demand mix is deteriorating even as volume hits records.** August visitor arrivals were a record 4.5m (+6.1%) but same-day visitors rose 11.7% while overnight visitors fell 2.4%; GGR per visitor fell 7% to MOP 4,888 (~$606) in August and is MOP 5,386 (~$667) for 8M-26, below both 2025 and pre-COVID. Hotel occupancy was 93.9% in August. The Macau Economic Association expects Q3-26 GDP −2% on the gaming slowdown.

**China policy is the overhang.** Seaport links premium softness to weaker mainland macro and tax enforcement on offshore trusts/wealth; CreditSights sees capital controls as a sentiment drag on high rollers but not a direct GGR hit because funding channels are already tightly controlled. Four of the six concessionaires flagged premium volume diversion during the World Cup.

**Junkets are structurally marginal.** Law 16/2022 confines gaming promoters to one concessionaire each, bans revenue-sharing and caps commissions at 1.25% of rolling; the gaming-credit law (effective Aug 2024) reserves credit extension to concessionaires. The budgeted MOP 150m (~$18.6m) junket-commission tax implies commissionable rolling of ~MOP 12bn (~$1.5bn) a year at the cap — a rounding error against VIP GGR of MOP 52bn+. Licensed junket count for 2026 is [unverified in this session].

**Enforcement is tightening, not loosening.** Gaming-related crime rose 12.3% in 9M-26; Law 7/2024 (effective Oct 2024) criminalised illegal currency exchange for gambling and strengthened sanctions on illegal/online gambling; casino entry is 21+, smoking is confined to non-gaming lounges, and gaming advertising is tightly restricted in Macau and criminalised for mainland audiences under PRC law.

**Non-gaming obligations are large and binding.** The six concessions carry MOP 118.8bn (~$14.7bn) of pledged investment (Galaxy alone MOP 28.35bn/~$3.5bn, of which only MOP 0.9bn/~$0.11bn gaming), with a +20% uplift once annual GGR exceeds MOP 180bn (~$22.3bn) — a trigger already met in 2024 (FY24 GGR MOP 226.8bn/~$28.1bn); the incremental amount is [unverified in this session].

**Read-through for B2Tech:** there is no B2C route into Macau before 2033 and no online route at all. The addressable opportunity is B2B — EGM/ETG cabinets, slot content, systems and compliance tech to six well-capitalised concessionaires chasing a slot segment growing ~19% a year in a market where everything else is flat-to-down; the 12,000-machine cap and MOP 300,000 (~$37k) minimum yield per machine shape the floor-space economics. Regional spill-over (Philippines, Vietnam, UAE 2027, Thailand if legalised) is the better B2C lens for the same customer base.

segments.name: Mass market (mass & premium-mass baccarat, other tables, electronic tables)
segments.headline: Mass baccarat −7.9% YoY to MOP 33.61bn (~$4.17bn) is the whole story of the quarter: record footfall, falling spend per head.
narrative: **Mass baccarat GGR fell to MOP 33.61bn (~$4.17bn), −7.9% YoY and −4.4% QoQ**, a third straight sequential decline from MOP 36.56bn (~$4.53bn) in Q1-26 and MOP 35.2bn (~$4.36bn) in Q2-26. DICJ's 'mass baccarat' bundles grind mass and premium mass; the operators' commentary and the sell-side both locate the weakness in premium mass, where the World Cup (11 Jun–19 Jul) diverted play and where Chinese high-end demand has softened under weaker macro and tighter tax enforcement on offshore wealth. The MOP 2.88bn (~$357m) YoY fall in this line was larger than the MOP 2.38bn (~$295m) fall in total GGR.

**The broader mass segment including slots fell 5.2% YoY to MOP 43.31bn (~$5.37bn), 71.9% of GGR**, versus MOP 45.13bn (~$5.59bn) in Q2-26 (+0.8% YoY then) and MOP 46.48bn (~$5.76bn) in Q1-26. Stripping out mass baccarat and slots leaves a residual of ~MOP 5.61bn (~$0.70bn) for other mass tables (sic bo, roulette, fan tan, blackjack, poker variants etc.), down ~2.6% YoY on our derivation; within that, live multi-game electronic terminals fell 8.0% to MOP 1.14bn (~$0.14bn) from MOP 1.30bn (~$0.16bn) in Q2 — notable because LMG had been a growth product and is where ETG suppliers compete.

**Volume is not the problem; yield is.** August visitor arrivals hit a record 4.5m (+6.1% YoY), hotel occupancy was 93.9%, yet GGR per visitor fell 7% to MOP 4,888 (~$606) and sits at MOP 5,386 (~$667) for 8M-26 — below both 2025 and pre-COVID. The Macau Economic Association attributes the gap to a mix shift: same-day visitors +11.7% while overnight visitors fell 2.4% in August. Concerts at Galaxy Arena and Venetian Arena lifted premium visitation in early August, which shows the non-gaming calendar can move premium mass at the margin but does not offset a cyclical downturn in Chinese wealth sentiment.

**Hold and comps.** Q3-25 was a high-hold quarter for several operators, so part of the −7.9% is a base effect; Seaport flags the tough hold comparison persisting into October. Even so, the two-quarter run of sequential declines (−3.8% then −4.4%) is a demand signal rather than a variance artefact, and the Macau Economic Association's estimate of Q3-26 GDP −2% confirms gaming is now a drag on the territory's economy.

**Commercial implication.** Mass is where the six concessionaires earn their margin (no junket commissions, lower reinvestment), so a 5–8% mass decline compresses EBITDA faster than the headline; CLSA and Goldman expect Q3 property EBITDA to fall YoY. For a supplier, the practical read is that operators will protect premium-mass floors with product refreshes and ETG/slot capacity (where yield per square metre is rising) rather than add tables under a 6,000-table cap and a MOP 7m (~$0.87m) per-table minimum-yield rule. Any mass-table capacity reallocation to electronic formats benefits machine and systems vendors.

segments.name: VIP baccarat & gaming promoters (junkets)
segments.headline: VIP GGR MOP 16.91bn (~$2.10bn) stabilised (+6.3% QoQ, flat YoY) under an in-house premium-direct model; junkets are now a residual channel.
narrative: **VIP baccarat GGR was MOP 16.91bn (~$2.10bn), +0.1% YoY and +6.3% QoQ**, recovering part of the 18.8% sequential collapse in Q2-26 (MOP 15.90bn/~$1.97bn, which analysts attributed to low hold and the World Cup) but still 13.6% below the Q1-26 peak of MOP 19.56bn (~$2.42bn, +35.4% YoY). Share of GGR rose to 28.1% (26.1% in Q2; 27.0% in Q3-25). For 9M-26 VIP GGR is MOP 52.38bn (~$6.49bn), +9.9% YoY, decelerating from +15.2% at the half-year.

**Definitional caveat.** DICJ classifies VIP by table designation inside the integrated resorts; the concessionaires' own disclosures report VIP/rolling-chip as a much smaller share of revenue (low-to-mid teens in most cases). The regulator's 'VIP' therefore captures a large slice of premium-direct play that operators book as premium mass. Comparisons with pre-2022 junket-era VIP (then ~50%+ of GGR) are not like-for-like.

**The junket channel has been legislated into irrelevance.** Law 16/2022 (in force with the new concessions) restricts each gaming promoter to a single concessionaire, bans revenue-share arrangements, caps commissions at 1.25% of rolling-chip turnover, and requires junket licensing with annual renewal; the gaming-credit law (effective Aug 2024) permits only concessionaires to extend gaming credit. The 2026 budget projects junket-commission tax of just MOP 150m (~$18.6m) — if that is levied on commissions at the 1.25% cap, it implies commissionable rolling of only ~MOP 12bn (~$1.5bn) a year [derived; the exact tax base is not confirmed]. The number of licensed promoters for 2026 could not be verified in this session.

**Macro and policy overhang.** CreditSights (29 Sep) argues China's capital-control tightening is unlikely to hit GGR directly because funding channels into Macau are already tightly policed, but could dampen high-roller sentiment; Seaport (early Oct) cites enforcement of tax on offshore trusts and weaker mainland macro as drags on wealthy customers. Citi's weekly checks in July showed VIP rolling volume up only 0–2% WoW even as the World Cup schedule thinned. Both point to VIP being range-bound rather than re-accelerating.

**Commercial implication.** VIP is now a concessionaire-owned, credit-backed premium-direct business; there is no third-party operator or agent model for a new entrant to plug into. The segment's value for a supplier is indirect — premium rooms drive demand for high-limit ETG and table-management/AML systems — and the regulatory direction (credit law, illegal-exchange crackdown, PRC cross-border gambling criminalisation) is unambiguously toward fewer intermediaries and more surveillance.

segments.name: Slots/EGMs, sports lottery and the (absent) online channel
segments.headline: Slots +18.8% YoY to MOP 4.09bn (~$0.51bn) are the only structural growth line; Macau Slot football GGR +49% on the World Cup; no online channel exists or is planned.
narrative: **Slot machine GGR grew 18.8% YoY to MOP 4.09bn (~$0.51bn)** (−0.5% QoQ from MOP 4.11bn/~$0.51bn), lifting share to 6.8% of GGR from 5.5% a year earlier; the quarterly growth run is +21.6% (Q1), +17.0% (Q2), +18.8% (Q3), giving 9M-26 slot GGR of MOP 12.18bn (~$1.51bn), ~+19% on our derivation. Growth is coming from premium-mass players migrating to high-denomination cabinets and smoke-free electronic floors, and from operators' active floor re-mixing, not from volume tourism (same-day visitors are rising, but their spend is low).

**Capacity economics favour machines.** The concession contracts cap the market at 12,000 machines (Venetian 3,700 and Galaxy 1,700 of the allocation, per the 2022 contract summaries) with a variable premium of MOP 1,000 (~$124) per machine and a minimum-yield test of MOP 300,000 (~$37k) GGR per machine per year, versus MOP 150,000–300,000 (~$18.6k–37k) premium and a MOP 7m (~$0.87m) minimum yield per table. At the current run-rate the installed base is yielding well above the minimum on average, so the cap, not the yield test, is the binding constraint — which supports replacement-cycle and premium-cabinet demand rather than unit expansion. Live multi-game ETGs, by contrast, fell 8.0% to MOP 1.14bn (~$0.14bn), suggesting operators are prioritising true slots over stadium-style ETG.

**Sports lottery is tiny and monopoly-run.** Macau Slot (SLOT) holds the sports-lottery concession for football and basketball; Q3-26 football GGR rose 49.0% to MOP 152m (~$18.8m) with the World Cup final on 19 July inside the quarter, and basketball GGR rose 4.8% to MOP 44m (~$5.5m). Together they are ~0.3% of casino GGR. The Macau Jockey Club ended horse racing in 2024, so pari-mutuel wagering is effectively nil. These numbers show how little Macau's regulated non-casino betting captures of local and visitor sports interest — the World Cup moved ~MOP 1–2bn (~$0.12–0.25bn) of casino GGR per month but only ~MOP 50m (~$6m) of lottery GGR.

**Online: zero and not on the agenda.** Macau licenses no online casino, poker or sports betting; Law 7/2024 (effective Oct 2024) sharpened criminal sanctions on illegal gambling including online promotion and illegal currency exchange tied to gambling, and the PRC criminalised organising cross-border gambling for mainland residents in 2021. DICJ maintains a public list of illegal gambling websites. Online penetration of the regulated market is therefore 0%, and there is no legislative initiative to change that; the political priority is economic diversification ('1+4'), not channel expansion.

**Commercial implication.** For B2Tech, the slot line is the only part of the Macau P&L growing double digits, and it is served through six buyers with regulator-approved EGM technical standards (DICJ EGM certification). The sports-lottery concession is a monopoly, and online is closed — so sportsbook or iGaming product has no legal landing in Macau; the relevant Asian online opportunities sit outside the SAR (Philippines PIGO, etc.).

segments.name: Licensing & tax: the concession regime (Law 16/2001 as amended by Law 7/2022)
segments.headline: Six 10-year concessions to 31 Dec 2032, 35% special tax + 5% fixed levies = 40% of GGR, premiums and minimum-yield rules — stable, closed and expensive.
narrative: **Structure.** Casino gaming is a government concession under Law 16/2001, comprehensively amended by Law 7/2022; the regulator is the Gaming Inspection and Coordination Bureau (DICJ) under the Secretary for Economy and Finance, with the Chief Executive (Sam Hou Fai since Dec 2024) holding the key discretionary powers. Six concessions were awarded by public tender in December 2022 — SJM Resorts, Galaxy Casino, Venetian Macau (Sands China), Wynn Resorts (Macau), Melco Resorts (Macau) and MGM Grand Paradise — each running 1 Jan 2023 to 31 Dec 2032. Sub-concessions were abolished; the maximum term is 10 years with exceptional extensions of up to three years at the Chief Executive's discretion. Concessionaires must have minimum share capital of MOP 5bn (~$0.62bn) and a Macau-permanent-resident managing director holding at least 15% of the capital; gaming may only be conducted in concessionaire-owned premises, which ended the satellite-casino model after a transition period to 31 Dec 2025 (a number of satellites closed at that deadline; the exact count is [unverified in this session]).

**Tax base and rate.** The special gaming tax is 35% of GGR (art. 27), payable monthly by the 10th of the following month to the Financial Services Bureau. On top, concessionaires pay 2% of GGR to a public foundation and 3% of GGR for urban development, tourism promotion and social security — Law 7/2022 deleted the previous 'up to' language under which the levies had in practice been charged at 1.6% and 2.4%, so the effective charge rose from 39% to a fixed 40% of GGR from 2023. Under AR 54/2022 the government may reduce or waive the 5% on GGR generated from foreign (non-mainland/HK/Taiwan) players as a diversification incentive — effectively 35% on that revenue. Gaming profits are exempt from the 12% complementary (profits) tax by dispatch covering 1 Jan 2023–31 Dec 2027; renewal is the next fiscal decision point. Junket commissions attract a separate withholding (budgeted at MOP 150m/~$18.6m for 2026).

**Premiums and minimum yield.** Each concessionaire pays a fixed annual premium of MOP 30m (~$3.7m) plus a variable premium of MOP 300,000 (~$37k) per VIP table, MOP 150,000 (~$18.6k) per mass table and MOP 1,000 (~$124) per machine, with a floor equal to 500 tables and 1,000 machines. If annual GGR per table falls below MOP 7m (~$0.87m) or per machine below MOP 300,000 (~$37k), a 'special premium' of 35% of the shortfall is due — in effect a minimum tax per unit of capacity, reviewable by the Chief Executive. Market-wide inventory is capped at 6,000 tables and 12,000 machines, allocated per concession (e.g., Venetian 1,680 tables/3,700 machines; Galaxy 1,000/1,700). A separate annual 'utilisation fee' is charged for casino space that reverted to the government on 31 Dec 2022.

**Fiscal dependence and take.** Gaming taxes were MOP 74.56bn (~$9.24bn) in 9M-26, +5.9% YoY (tax lags GGR by a month, so this reflects Dec-25–Aug-26 GGR), equal to 84.1% of MOP 88.71bn (~$10.99bn) government current revenue; the 2026 budget expects MOP 92.53bn (~$11.47bn) of gaming taxes (MOP 82.60bn/~$10.24bn from the 35% special tax) on an assumed GGR of MOP 236bn (~$29.2bn). Applying 40% to Q3-26 GGR implies ~MOP 24.1bn (~$2.99bn) of quarterly levies before premiums [derived]. That dependence cuts both ways: it is why the government will not raise the rate (the 40% is already the highest headline casino tax among major jurisdictions) and why it leans on concessionaires for non-gaming investment instead — MOP 118.8bn (~$14.7bn) pledged across the six contracts, with a +20% uplift triggered once annual GGR exceeds MOP 180bn (~$22.3bn), which happened in 2024.

**Direction of travel.** No change to rates, caps or the number of concessions is on the table before 2032. The live items are: (i) the 2027 Policy Address and budget (Nov 2026), which will set a new GGR assumption and may revisit the foreign-player levy waiver; (ii) renewal of the profits-tax exemption beyond 2027; (iii) DICJ's ongoing scrutiny of non-gaming investment delivery and of the post-satellite footprint; (iv) possible tightening of the minimum-yield thresholds if GGR per table stays below 2019 levels. For an operator, the regime offers unusual contractual certainty but no entry route; for a supplier it offers six solvent, tax-paying buyers who are contractually obliged to keep investing.

segments.name: Payments, AML, responsible gambling, advertising & enforcement
segments.headline: A cash-and-chip market inside China's capital-control perimeter, with enforcement intensity rising (gaming-related crime +12.3% in 9M-26) and no advertising runway.
narrative: **Payments reality.** Macau is a HKD-chip, cash-settled casino market; there is no licensed online wallet layer because there is no online gambling. Mainland visitors operate under PRC foreign-exchange rules (the US$50,000 annual individual quota and UnionPay card controls), Macau's cross-border cash declaration regime, and now Law 7/2024 (effective Oct 2024), which criminalised unlicensed currency exchange for gambling purposes — the 'money-changer' gangs that historically funded premium play. CreditSights' September note is explicit that funding channels are already so tightly controlled that incremental Chinese capital-control tightening is unlikely to show up in GGR directly. Casino credit may be extended only by concessionaires under the gaming-credit law (effective Aug 2024); junkets and third parties are excluded. Digital-yuan or card-at-cage innovations are not a feature of the regulated gaming floor [status unverified in this session].

**AML/KYC.** Concessionaires file large-transaction and suspicious-transaction reports to the Financial Intelligence Office (GIF) under DICJ AML instructions; the 2022–2024 legislative package (gaming law, junket law, credit law, illegal-gambling law) collectively shifted liability onto the concessionaires and removed the intermediaries that previously absorbed it. Gaming-related crime rose 12.3% in 9M-26 per Macau police data reported by IAG, which — combined with four months of GGR declines — argues for continued aggressive enforcement rather than relaxation.

**Responsible gambling.** Casino entry and employment are restricted to persons aged 21+ (Law 10/2012); DICJ administers self-exclusion and third-party exclusion schemes; smoking is permitted only in enclosed smoking lounges with no gaming (full-floor ban since 2019); and the government's 'responsible gambling' programme runs through DICJ and the Social Welfare Bureau. Published 2026 self-exclusion or problem-gambling prevalence figures could not be verified in this session.

**Advertising.** Gambling advertising is heavily restricted in Macau under the general advertising law, and the material constraint is external: PRC Criminal Law (Art. 303, amended 2021) criminalises organising or soliciting mainland residents for cross-border gambling, so no concessionaire markets gaming to the mainland; promotion is confined to non-gaming (concerts, MICE, F&B, hotels) — which is exactly where the 2H26 event calendar is being used to pull premium visitation.

**Commercial implication.** The compliance perimeter is tighter than in any Western market a B2B supplier would normally serve: product must pass DICJ technical certification, payments innovation on the floor is effectively off-limits, and any marketing or affiliate activity aimed at Chinese players is a criminal exposure. The upside is that compliance technology (surveillance, KYC/STR automation, table-management, chip tracking) is a growing procurement line for six well-funded buyers.

highlights.text: Slots are a structural growth line: GGR +18.8% YoY to MOP 4.09bn (~$0.51bn) in Q3-26 and ~+19% for 9M-26 (MOP 12.18bn/~$1.51bn), with share up to 6.8% — the one product the six concessionaires are actively expanding under a 12,000-machine cap, which sustains premium-cabinet replacement demand for EGM suppliers.

Demand volume is at record levels — 4.5m visitors in August (+6.1%), 93.9% hotel occupancy — so the market's problem is yield mix, not footfall; a stabilisation in Chinese high-end sentiment would flow straight to premium-mass GGR.

Regulatory certainty is unusually high: the 35% + 5% = 40% GGR levy, premiums, inventory caps and six concessions are contractually fixed to 31 Dec 2032, and the profits-tax exemption runs to end-2027; there is no live proposal to raise rates.

The government's FY26 GGR assumption of MOP 236bn (~$29.2bn) needs only MOP 48.9bn (~$6.06bn) in Q4 — a very low bar — and gaming taxes are already +5.9% YoY at MOP 74.56bn (~$9.24bn), removing any fiscal pressure for a tax or premium increase.

VIP has found a floor: +6.3% QoQ to MOP 16.91bn (~$2.10bn) and +9.9% for 9M-26, now run premium-direct by concessionaires with credit under their own control — a cleaner, higher-margin structure than the junket era.

The non-gaming calendar works: concerts at Galaxy and Venetian arenas visibly lifted premium visitation in early August, and MOP 118.8bn (~$14.7bn) of contractually pledged investment keeps the integrated-resort product improving through 2032.

Six solvent, tax-paying buyers with mandatory DICJ product certification create a concentrated but durable B2B channel for EGMs, ETGs, systems and compliance technology — the only realistic Macau entry for a non-concessionaire.

lowlights.text: Closed market: no new concession before 2033, sub-concessions abolished, satellites wound down, and no online licensing of any kind — there is no B2C route for an outside operator, and the sports-lottery is a single-concession monopoly.

Mass/premium-mass baccarat fell 7.9% YoY and 4.4% QoQ to MOP 33.61bn (~$4.17bn) with GGR per visitor down 7% to MOP 4,888 (~$606); the two-quarter sequential decline signals demand, not variance, and compresses operator EBITDA faster than headline GGR.

Chinese policy overhang: tax enforcement on offshore trusts/wealth and capital-control tightening are cited by Seaport and CreditSights as drags on high-end demand; four consecutive monthly YoY declines (Jun–Sep) and FY26 growth consensus cut to ~1–3% from 7%.

The world's highest headline casino levy — 40% of GGR plus fixed/variable premiums, a 35%-of-shortfall minimum-yield premium (MOP 7m/~$0.87m per table) and MOP 118.8bn (~$14.7bn) of mandated non-gaming capex — leaves thin margin for error if GGR stays ~15% below 2019.

Enforcement intensity is rising, not falling: gaming-related crime +12.3% in 9M-26, criminalised currency exchange (Law 7/2024), concessionaire-only credit, and PRC criminal exposure for any marketing to mainland players — compliance cost and legal risk are structurally high for any vendor or partner.

Data definitions are unreliable for modelling: DICJ's 'VIP' (28.1% of GGR) is far above the concessionaires' own VIP disclosures, and trade-press 9M totals diverge (MOP 187.1bn vs a mislabelled 181.3bn); operator-level market shares are not published by the regulator.

Regional competition for the same Chinese premium customer is building — UAE (Wynn Al Marjan, 2027), Philippines and Singapore today, Thailand and Japan (Osaka, 2030) later — while Macau's product is 84% baccarat and cannot add online.

forecast.intro: The official FY26 anchor is the budget's MOP 236bn (~$29.2bn) GGR assumption, reaffirmed by Chief Executive Sam Hou Fai on 10 Oct pending October data; it is a fiscal floor rather than a forecast, since 9M-26 GGR of MOP 187.1bn (~$23.2bn) leaves only MOP 48.9bn (~$6.06bn) to find in Q4 against a Q4-25 base of ~MOP 66.1bn (~$8.19bn). The sell-side has moved the other way: J.P. Morgan now has FY26 at MOP 249bn (~$30.9bn, +1%), Seaport models Q4 −5%, and one bank has October −6% at MOP 22.6bn (~$2.80bn). The swing is entirely in mass/premium-mass baccarat — VIP is flat and slots are adding ~MOP 0.6bn (~$75m) a quarter YoY — and is driven by Chinese high-end demand (macro, offshore-wealth tax enforcement, capital controls) and tough hold comps rather than anything regulatory.

forecast.view: **Market:** our base case is FY26 GGR of ~MOP 250bn (~$31.0bn), +1% (estimate), with Q4 down ~5% on tough hold comps and soft premium mass; a flat Q4 would give ~MOP 253bn (~$31.4bn, +2.3%) and −8% would give ~MOP 248bn (~$30.7bn, +0.2%). Comps ease materially from Q2-27 (World Cup base) and the 2027 calendar lacks a comparable sporting drag, so we expect a return to **low-single-digit growth in 2027**, still ~15% below 2019 — with **slots compounding mid-teens** and mass baccarat flat-to-down until Chinese wealth sentiment turns. **Margins:** operator EBITDA falls faster than GGR in 2H26 (CLSA/Goldman), and the 40% levy plus minimum-yield premiums make the government's take almost fully variable-proof; expect gaming tax of ~MOP 99–100bn (~$12.3–12.4bn) for FY26 (estimate, 40% × GGR), well above the MOP 92.53bn (~$11.47bn) budget. **Rules:** no change to the 35%/40% rate, the six concessions or the inventory caps before 2032; the 2027 Policy Address (Nov 2026) will reset the GGR assumption (likely ~MOP 240–250bn/~$29.7–31.0bn, estimate) and may expand the foreign-player levy waiver as a diversification tool; the profits-tax exemption is likely renewed beyond 2027. **Enforcement direction is one-way tighter** — expect further action on illegal exchange, cross-border online gambling and junket residue, and closer DICJ auditing of non-gaming investment delivery. **For B2Tech:** treat Macau as a B2B-only, slot-and-systems opportunity with six buyers, and as the demand bellwether for Chinese premium play across Asia — not as a licensing target.
watch: October 2026 DICJ monthly GGR (1 Nov) and the CE's stated decision point on the MOP 236bn (~$29.2bn) forecast; Q4 needs only MOP 16.3bn (~$2.02bn)/month.
Concessionaire Q3-26 results (late Oct–early Nov): property EBITDA margins, premium-mass commentary, reported VIP vs DICJ's 28.1% share, and any disclosure of operator GGR shares.
2027 Policy Address and budget (Nov 2026): new GGR assumption, profits-tax exemption renewal (expires 31 Dec 2027), foreign-player 5% levy waiver, and non-gaming investment compliance.
PRC policy: offshore-income/trust tax enforcement, capital-control measures, UnionPay/cash rules, and any change in Individual Visit Scheme coverage or visa facilitation.
DICJ enforcement cadence: illegal currency-exchange prosecutions under Law 7/2024, junket licence renewals for 2027, and the post-satellite casino footprint (tables/slots vs the 6,000/12,000 caps).
Regional competition milestones: UAE commercial gaming (Wynn Al Marjan, 2027), Thailand entertainment-complex legislation, and Philippine/Singapore premium-mass trends.

report.confidenceNote: FX: USD/MOP ~8.07 as of 30 Sep 2026 (MOP is pegged to HKD at 1.03; rate implied by contemporaneous press conversions of DICJ data, e.g. MOP 60.22bn = US$7.46bn). Confidence MEDIUM: headline Q3-26, Q2-26, Q1-26 and monthly GGR figures are DICJ data relayed identically by four independent trade outlets (IAG, AGB, Focus GN, Yogonet/WCD) and reconcile to within MOP 0.01bn across monthly and quarterly series, but the DICJ statistical tables themselves could not be loaded in this session (fetch quota). Fiscal figures are from the Financial Services Bureau via GGRAsia/IAG; concession/tax rules are from the Wynn Macau HKEX concession announcement, the 2022 contract summaries, Chambers and PwC. Items derived by calculation are labelled 'derived'. Not verified in this session: licensed junket count, table/slot counts and casino count at 30 Sep 2026, satellite-casino closures, operator market shares, the incremental non-gaming investment amount after the MOP 180bn trigger, and 2026 self-exclusion statistics — all marked n/a or [unverified]. One source (Focus GN) reports 9M-26 GGR as MOP 181.3bn/+3.7%; this equals the 9M-25 base and is treated as mislabelled; the MOP 187.1bn/+3.2% figure (IAG, Asia Casino) is used.
